title: The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I, Prelude no. 1 in C major
source_citations: Heinrich Schenker, Five Graphic Music Analyses (1933)
Donald Tovey, A Companion to Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier (1924)

key_plan.role: Tonicization of V (G major) then return — analytically still in C major (Schenkerian background)
Long dominant pedal (G) under chromatic upper-voice activity, resolving to final PAC

notable_cadences.basis: Half cadence on V — closes opening tonic prolongation

characteristic_features: Single broken-chord arpeggiation pattern throughout — no melody/accompaniment distinction
Famously diatonic — secondary dominants are the most adventurous chromatic feature
Influential as a study in pure harmonic progression; Schenker chose it for Five Graphic Music Analyses
common_omr_pitfalls: Arpeggiation pattern means chord pitches are spread across many beats — chordify may over-fragment chord boundaries
No real polyphony — voice splitting should be trivial; multiple detected voices in the OMR output suggests an OMR error rather than real voice independence
_notes: Curated 2026-05-24. Conservative encoding — only includes structural facts where Schenker / Tovey / Forte agree. Don't add Schenkerian middle-ground or foreground graph data here; that's M3+ if ever.
